notes: I recall this being sourced on Wikiquote's Helen Keller page to her 1929 book We Bereaved, with the original reading '...the one which has been opened for us.' The bare proverb 'when one door closes, another opens' is older and is often credited to Alexander Graham Bell (Keller's friend); Keller's contribution is the second clause about staring at the closed door. Confident in Keller as author, moderately confident in the 1929 book as the print locus.

Genuinely Keller. The full passage runs 'Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure or nothing.' Standard citation is The Open Door (1957); some sources instead point to Let Us Have Faith (1940). Author attribution is solid; I am less certain which of the two volumes is the first printing, so I am holding below verified.

From Creative Evolution, ch. 1. The original opens with a qualifier the corpus text drops: 'For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.' Primary source confirmed; only the truncation is at issue, and it does not alter the sense.

earliest_print_source: Journal Intime (Amiel's Journal), Henri-Frederic Amiel, trans. Mrs. Humphry Ward, 1885
notes: Amiel's aphorisms nearly all come from the Journal Intime, published posthumously and Englished by Mrs. Humphry Ward in 1885; this line reads as authentic Ward-translation Amiel and is consistently attributed to him. I cannot recall the dated journal entry it belongs to, so I am not claiming a page-level verification.

Consistently attributed to Amiel and stylistically of a piece with the Journal Intime, which is the source of essentially all circulating Amiel quotations. I cannot place the specific entry or confirm the translation used, so no print source is claimed.

Widely circulated under Matisse's name in quotation anthologies. I cannot place it in Notes of a Painter (1908), Jazz (1947), or the Flam collection of Matisse's writings, and the phrasing reads more like an English aphorism than a translation from Matisse's French. Plausible but unconfirmed; the sentiment about the resistance of the medium is genuinely Matissean, which is not evidence of authorship.

Genuine Thoreau, from the 'Higher Laws' chapter of Walden. The original reads 'a miracle which is taking place every instant' — the corpus text substitutes 'every second,' a common circulating variant. Recommend restoring 'instant' if the corpus prefers original wording.

I do not believe this paragraph appears anywhere in Thoreau. It reads as a later self-help expansion of a genuine passage in Walden's 'Conclusion': 'It is remarkable how easily and insensibly we fall into a particular route, and make a beaten track for ourselves... The surface of the earth is soft and impressible by the feet of men; and so with the paths which the mind travels.' The 'single footstep / single thought / think over and over the kind of thoughts we wish to dominate our lives' construction is characteristic of twentieth-century New Thought prose, not Thoreau's. I cannot name the actual writer who composed the expansion, so no reattribution is offered.
Verbatim Thoreau from the 'Conclusion' of Walden. Short, exact, and correctly attributed.

Both halves are genuine Walden, from 'Conclusion,' but the corpus text is the popular second-person paraphrase. Thoreau wrote in the third person: 'I learned this, at least, by my experiment: that if one advances confidently in the direction of his dreams, and endeavors to live the life which he has imagined, he will meet with a success unexpected in common hours.' The passage also compresses the original ('he will put some things behind, will pass an invisible boundary'; 'he will live with the license of a higher order of beings') and the castles line ends 'Now put the foundations under them,' plural. Source certain; wording modernized.

earliest_print_source: The Greatest Thing in the World, Henry Drummond, c. 1887
notes: Consistently attributed to Drummond's famous address on 1 Corinthians 13, delivered in the mid-1880s and printed as The Greatest Thing in the World. The sentiment and cadence match that text closely. I am not certain of the exact publication year (the address circulated from 1884 and the book appeared later in the decade) and cannot confirm the page, so the year above is approximate rather than a verified citation.

No evidence Ford ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator examined it and found no attribution to Ford during his lifetime; the earliest linkages surface in business and marketing literature around the turn of the twenty-first century, decades after his 1947 death. It does not appear in My Life and Work (1922). Wikiquote carries it as disputed/unsourced. No true originator is identifiable, so I am marking it apocryphal rather than reattributing.

The core sentence — 'the only real security a man can have in this world is a reserve of knowledge, experience and ability' — is very consistently attributed to Ford and is compatible with his views on money as a tool in My Life and Work (1922) and his Dearborn Independent pieces. I cannot place the full paragraph in a specific Ford text, and the surrounding sentences may be an anthologist's assembly. Plausibly genuine, unconfirmed; keeping it below the promotion bar.

Ford is a misattribution magnet, and this is one of the borderline cases. The saying does not appear in Ford's own writings as far as I know; the earliest attribution to him that I recall from Quote Investigator's treatment is a Reader's Digest filler item in 1947, the year Ford died — a secondhand ascription, not a source. Circulating wording is usually 'Whether you think you can, or you think you can't, you're right,' without the corpus text's 'probably.' Attribution is traditional rather than documented.

Known only as a reported remark, not as anything James published. The tradition traces to a recollection by James's nephew (Billy James), passed into the biographical literature and the collections of Jamesian anecdote; there is no primary text. It is also frequently confused with William James. Plausibly a real spoken remark, but unverifiable from what I know. Note that q_0716 is a near-duplicate of this entry, differing only by an 'And' — the corpus should keep one.

Duplicate of q_0715 with 'And the third' shortened to 'The third'; same verdict. Secondhand anecdote attributed to Henry James via his nephew's recollection, with no primary text and recurring confusion with William James. Recommend deduplicating against q_0715 and preferring whichever wording the source anthology used.

The form I have encountered is 'The full and joyful acceptance of the worst in oneself may be the only sure way of transforming it' — the corpus text has softened 'the worst in oneself' to 'the self' and hardened 'may be' to 'is,' which changes the meaning. Attributed to Henry Miller in quotation collections; I cannot place it in The Wisdom of the Heart, Big Sur and the Oranges of Hieronymus Bosch, or any other Miller volume. Uncertain both as to authorship and as to wording.

earliest_print_source: The Colossus of Maroussi, Henry Miller, 1941
notes: I am fairly confident this passage is from the closing pages of The Colossus of Maroussi, which contains the 'every moment is a golden one for him who has the vision to recognize it as such' line. The corpus text drops the 'it' in that final clause. Authorship confident; page-level citation not recalled, so short of verified.

Attributed to Miller across quotation sites, but I cannot locate it in any of his books and have no early citation for it. Possibly from an essay or interview, possibly an anthologist's condensation. Honest answer: I don't know where this comes from.

earliest_print_source: 'For Katrina's Sun-Dial,' Henry van Dyke, in Music and Other Poems, 1904
notes: Genuine van Dyke. Written as a sundial inscription for Katrina Trask at Yaddo and printed in his 1904 collection; the verse is set as short lines, which the corpus has run together as prose. Van Dyke wrote a second, shorter sundial verse ('Hours fly, flowers die...') that is sometimes conflated with this one.

Long and consistently attributed to van Dyke, and consonant with his essays, but I recall it sitting in the unsourced section of quotation references rather than being tied to a specific book or sermon. The usual wording includes 'no birds sang there except those that sang best,' which the corpus drops. Likely genuine, undocumented.

Attributed to van Dyke in anthologies; the homiletic register fits a Presbyterian preacher-essayist, and the line may come from a sermon or address. I cannot name the text, and I have no early citation. Unverified.

earliest_print_source: 'The Secret of the Sea,' Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, in The Seaside and the Fireside, 1850
notes: Genuine Longfellow, from the poem 'The Secret of the Sea.' The stanza is spoken in dialogue and the original is archaic: 'Wouldst thou' — so the helmsman answered — 'learn the secret of the sea? / Only those who brave its dangers / Comprehend its mystery!' The corpus text modernizes the opening and drops the helmsman frame. Poem attribution is certain; I am slightly less sure of the collecting volume, though The Seaside and the Fireside (1850) is my recollection.

Beecher's circulating aphorisms mostly derive from Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit (1887) and Life Thoughts (1858), compilations drawn from his preaching, and this line plausibly belongs to one of them. I cannot confirm which, or that it is Beecher's at all rather than a compiler's condensation of a longer passage. Unverified.

Very consistently attributed to Beecher and characteristic of his pulpit style; most likely from one of the Plymouth Pulpit compilations (Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit, 1887, or Life Thoughts, 1858). I cannot confirm the volume or page from memory, so no print source is claimed. Probably genuine but held below the promotion bar.
